los.text: Describe the impact of vascular disease and why knowledge is important for all doctors
los.html:
Burden
  • Cardiovascular disease (CHD, stroke, PAD, aneurysms, venous disease) is a leading cause of death and disability in the UK
  • PAD affects ~20% of over-60s (most asymptomatic)
  • Venous disease (varicose veins ~1 in 3 adults; venous leg ulcers ~1%)
  • Diabetes-related amputations rising.
Why every doctor needs to know
  • Atherosclerosis is systemic: PAD is a marker of high risk of MI/stroke (CV mortality ×3) → secondary prevention opportunity in any specialty.
  • Emergencies present everywhere: acute limb ischaemia (6 Ps), ruptured AAA (collapse with back/abdominal pain mimics renal colic), aortic dissection, DVT/PE, compartment syndrome, diabetic foot sepsis.
  • Chronic wounds (leg ulcers, diabetic feet) are common in primary care/community/ward patients; misdiagnosis (venous vs arterial) → harm (compression on ischaemic leg).
  • Vascular access (cannulas, central lines, arterial sampling), procedures (femoral puncture) and complications (pseudoaneurysm, embolism).
  • Risk factor management (smoking, diabetes, BP, lipids) is everyone's job.
  • Amputation has huge impact (mortality ~50% at 2–5 years after major amputation in diabetics).

los.text: Describe normal and abnormal arterial wall physiology and explain how this causes PAD (Peripheral Arterial Disease)
sessions: Physiology and Pathophysiology of the artery
los.html:
Normal arterial wall
  • Intima (endothelium on basement membrane: produces NO (vasodilator, anti-platelet, anti-proliferative), prostacyclin, endothelin; barrier; anticoagulant surface), media (smooth muscle + elastic lamellae: tone, compliance), adventitia (connective tissue, vasa vasorum, nerves).
  • Large elastic arteries buffer pressure (Windkessel)
  • Muscular arteries/arterioles regulate flow (resistance ∝ 1/r⁴).
Abnormal
  • Endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO, ↑ adhesion molecules, ↑ permeability)
  • → atherosclerosis (lipid entry and oxidation, foam cells, smooth muscle migration, fibrous cap, necrotic core, calcification)
  • → stenosis/occlusion of large and medium arteries (aorto-iliac, femoropopliteal, tibial), plaque rupture/thrombosis, embolism
  • Medial calcification (Mönckeberg: diabetes, CKD → stiff, incompressible arteries)
  • Arterial stiffening with age.
How this causes PAD
  • Fixed stenoses limit the increase in flow needed during exercise
  • → supply/demand mismatch in muscles distal to the lesion
  • → anaerobic metabolism, lactate
  • → intermittent claudication
  • Progressive narrowing/multi-level disease + poor collaterals → rest pain, tissue loss (ulcers, gangrene) = chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
  • Acute thrombosis/embolism → acute limb ischaemia.
  • Distal disease (tibial) prominent in diabetes and CKD.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology of disease states and what risk factors impact.
sessions: Physiology and Pathophysiology of the artery
los.html:
Atherosclerotic disease statesCHD, cerebrovascular disease, PAD, renovascular disease, mesenteric ischaemia, aneurysmal disease (degenerative wall weakening).
Risk factors and impact
  • Smoking: strongest for PAD (×2–4 risk; dose-dependent); endothelial damage, ↑ thrombosis, ↓ graft patency; stopping is the most important intervention.
  • Diabetes: ×2–4 PAD risk, distal (infrapopliteal) disease, medial calcification, combined with neuropathy and infection → ulcers/amputation.
  • Hypertension: endothelial shear stress, arterial stiffness; also AAA risk.
  • Dyslipidaemia (↑ LDL, ↓ HDL, ↑ Lp(a)).
  • Age, male sex, FHx, ethnicity (South Asian: CHD/diabetes; Black: PAD).
  • CKD (calcification), obesity, physical inactivity, raised homocysteine, inflammation (CRP).
Aneurysm risk factorsSmoking (strongest), male, age, FHx, hypertension, connective tissue disorders (diabetes is protective for AAA).
Venous disease risk factorsAge, female, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged standing, FHx, previous DVT.

los.text: Identify common presentation of patients with claudication and how they will be assessed and managed
sessions: Physiology and Pathophysiology of the artery
los.html:
Intermittent claudication
  • Cramping/aching pain in calf (± thigh/buttock) on walking a reproducible distance, relieved by standing still for a few minutes
  • Site indicates level (calf = femoropopliteal; buttock/thigh + erectile dysfunction = aorto-iliac: Leriche syndrome).
DifferentialsSpinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication: relieved by sitting/bending forward, variable distance, pain/numbness down legs), OA hip/knee, venous claudication, Baker's cyst, nerve root pain.
Assessment
  • History (walking distance, impact, risk factors, CV history)
  • Examination (pulses: femoral, popliteal, DP, PT; bruits; skin: hair loss, pallor, cool, Buerger's test, capillary refill; ulcers)
  • ABPI (<0.9 diagnostic; 0.5–0.9 claudication)
  • Toe pressures (diabetes)
  • Duplex ultrasound (site/severity)
  • CTA/MRA if intervention considered
  • Bloods (FBC, lipids, HbA1c, U&E).
Management (NICE CG147)
  • Best medical therapy: smoking cessation, antiplatelet (clopidogrel 75 mg; or aspirin; low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin in selected), high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), BP and diabetes control, weight, foot care.
  • Supervised exercise programme (2 h/week for 3 months; walk to near-maximal pain): first-line; improves walking distance.
  • Naftidrofuryl (vasodilator) if exercise unsatisfactory and patient doesn't want revascularisation.
  • Revascularisation (angioplasty ± stent, bypass) if symptoms persist despite exercise and lifestyle significantly impaired.
PrognosisLimb generally stable (~1–2%/year progress to amputation) but CV death risk high (stroke, MI).

los.text: Describe the presentation, investigation and management of critical limb ischaemia.
los.html:
Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI, formerly critical limb ischaemia)
  • PAD with ischaemic rest pain (>2 weeks)
  • Non-healing ulcers or gangrene (tissue loss)
  • Ankle pressure typically <50 mmHg or toe pressure <30
  • ABPI often <0.5 (falsely normal/high in calcified arteries).
Presentation
  • Rest pain in the forefoot/toes, worse at night/elevation, relieved by hanging the leg out of bed or sleeping in a chair (gravity)
  • Dependent rubor ("sunset foot")
  • Pallor on elevation (Buerger's angle <20°)
  • Cold
  • Hairless shiny skin
  • Thickened nails
  • Absent pulses
  • Arterial ulcers (painful, punched-out, toes/heels/pressure points)
  • Dry or wet gangrene.
Investigations
  • ABPI and toe pressures/TcPO₂, duplex ultrasound, CT angiography (or MRA/digital subtraction angiography) for planning
  • Bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, HbA1c, lipids), wound swabs, X-ray (osteomyelitis), ECG/echo (embolic source, fitness for surgery).
Management (urgent vascular referral, MDT)
  • Analgesia (often opioids)
  • Revascularisation (endovascular angioplasty/stenting or surgical bypass (vein graft) or endarterectomy)
  • Best medical therapy
  • Wound care
  • Infection treatment (antibiotics, debridement)
  • Podiatry/offloading
  • Diabetic control
  • Amputation if unsalvageable
  • Palliative care in some.
PrognosisHigh risk of amputation and death (~25% mortality at 1 year).

los.text: Explain when amputation is necessary
los.html:
Indications for amputation
  • Dead (non-viable) limb: extensive gangrene/necrosis, irreversible acute ischaemia (fixed mottling, paralysis, rigor).
  • Dangerous limb: life-threatening infection (wet gangrene, necrotising fasciitis, diabetic foot sepsis with spreading infection, gas gangrene), malignancy (sarcoma).
  • "Dead loss" limb: unreconstructable CLTI with intractable rest pain despite maximal therapy, non-healing wounds where revascularisation impossible or has failed, a useless limb (severe contractures, neuropathic), severe trauma (mangled extremity).
Levels
  • Minor (toes, transmetatarsal, ray) vs major (below-knee (preferred for rehabilitation/prosthesis; requires adequate perfusion for healing), above-knee, through-knee)
  • Level chosen by perfusion, infection extent, functional potential.
Considerations
  • Patient's goals, mobility, rehabilitation potential, prosthetic fitting, phantom limb pain, psychological impact, MDT (vascular surgeon, rehab, physio/OT, prosthetist, diabetologist, psychology)
  • High perioperative mortality in elderly/comorbid.

los.text: Describe the differences between acute and chronic ischaemia
los.html:
Acute limb ischaemiaChronic limb ischaemia
OnsetSudden (<2 weeks; usually hours)Gradual (months–years)
CauseEmbolus (AF, MI mural thrombus, aneurysm) or thrombosis in situ (on pre-existing atheroma, graft occlusion), trauma, dissection, popliteal aneurysmProgressive atherosclerosis
CollateralsAbsent (embolus) → severe ischaemiaDeveloped → compensation
Features6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis (last two = threatened limb)Claudication → rest pain → ulcers/gangrene; hair loss, shiny skin, thick nails
Contralateral limbNormal pulses suggest embolismOften bilateral disease
UrgencyEmergency: irreversible damage within ~6 hUrgent (CLTI) or routine (claudication)
Management
  • IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia, urgent vascular surgery: embolectomy (Fogarty catheter), thrombolysis, bypass, angioplasty
  • Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome after reperfusion
  • Reperfusion injury (hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria/AKI)
  • Amputation if irreversible
  • Anticoagulation long-term if embolic (AF)
Best medical therapy, exercise, revascularisation as indicated
  • Rutherford classification of acute ischaemia: I viable
    • IIa marginally threatened
    • IIb immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond toes, mild weakness)
    • III irreversible (profound paralysis, fixed staining).

los.text: Explain why abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) develop
los.html:
AAAAbdominal aorta diameter ≥3 cm (≥1.5× normal); usually infrarenal.
Pathogenesis
  • Degenerative (not simply atherosclerotic): chronic inflammation of the aortic wall (macrophages, lymphocytes)
  • → matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9) degrade elastin and collagen in the media
  • → ↓ smooth muscle cells (apoptosis)
  • → weakening and dilatation
  • Laplace's law (wall tension ∝ pressure × radius) → as diameter increases, tension increases → further expansion and rupture.
  • Infrarenal aorta has fewer elastic lamellae and lacks vasa vasorum.
Risk factors
  • Smoking (strongest; continued smoking ↑ growth)
  • Male sex (×4–6)
  • Age >65
  • FHx (first-degree relative)
  • Hypertension
  • COPD
  • Atherosclerosis
  • Connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos)
  • Caucasian
  • Diabetes is protective.
Other causesMycotic (infection), inflammatory, trauma, syphilis (thoracic).

los.text: Recall the screening programme for AAAs
los.html:
• NHS AAA Screening Programme (Wales AAA Screening Programme): one-off abdominal ultrasound for men in the year they turn 65
    • men >65 can self-refer.
    • (Based on MASS trial: ~50% ↓ AAA-related mortality.) Women not routinely screened (lower prevalence, rupture at smaller sizes).
Aortic diameterResult and action
<3.0 cmNormal: discharged
3.0–4.4 cm (small)Annual ultrasound surveillance
4.5–5.4 cm (medium)3-monthly surveillance
≥5.5 cm (large)Refer to vascular surgeon within 2 weeks (consider repair)
  • Surveillance includes: smoking cessation
    • BP control
    • statin + antiplatelet (CV risk)
    • advice about symptoms (sudden abdominal/back pain → 999)
    • driving rules (DVLA: notify ≥6 cm; stop driving ≥6.5 cm; Group 2 stop ≥5.5 cm).

los.text: Describe the management of AAAs
los.html:
Small AAA (<5.5 cm)Surveillance (as screening intervals), risk factor modification (smoking cessation, BP, statin, aspirin), exercise.
Elective repair indications
  • ≥5.5 cm, growth >1 cm/year, or symptomatic (tender, abdominal/back pain) aneurysm.
  • EVAR (endovascular aneurysm repair): stent graft via femoral arteries; lower perioperative mortality, quicker recovery; needs suitable anatomy (neck length/angle) and lifelong surveillance (endoleaks: type II commonest, graft migration); reinterventions.
  • Open repair: laparotomy, aortic cross-clamp, synthetic graft; higher early mortality (~3–5%) but durable; for younger fit patients/unsuitable anatomy.
  • NICE NG156 (2020): open repair preferred for many unless contraindicated (EVAR cost-effectiveness concerns); decision individualised.
Ruptured AAA
  • Collapse, severe abdominal/back/flank pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass
  • Mortality ~80% overall.
  • Management: immediate vascular surgical referral
  • Permissive hypotension (SBP ~70–90; avoid excessive fluids)
  • Large-bore access
  • Crossmatch (major haemorrhage protocol)
  • CT angiography if stable
  • Emergency EVAR or open repair
  • Consider palliation if unfit.
Complications of repairMI, AKI, colonic ischaemia (IMA), spinal cord ischaemia, distal embolism ("trash foot"), graft infection, endoleak, aorto-enteric fistula.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology of veins in healthy and diseased states
los.html:
Normal venous physiology
  • Low pressure, high compliance (capacitance vessels: ~70% of blood volume)
  • One-way bicuspid valves prevent reflux
  • Superficial veins drain to deep veins via perforators and junctions (saphenofemoral, saphenopopliteal)
  • Return to heart driven by calf muscle pump (soleal sinuses compressed during walking → ankle venous pressure falls from ~90 mmHg standing to ~20–30 mmHg walking), respiratory pump, foot pump, vis a tergo
  • Venous tone (sympathetic).
Diseased states
  • Valvular incompetence (primary: weak walls/valves, genetics; secondary: post-thrombotic valve damage after DVT) → reflux → ambulatory venous hypertension (pressure stays high during walking).
  • Obstruction (DVT, May–Thurner iliac compression, tumour) → impaired outflow.
  • Calf muscle pump failure (immobility, ankle stiffness, neuromuscular disease, obesity).
Consequences of venous hypertension
  • Distension → varicose veins
  • Capillary leak → oedema, RBC extravasation → haemosiderin deposition (brown staining)
  • Inflammation and fibrosis → lipodermatosclerosis, venous eczema, atrophie blanche → venous ulceration.
  • Spectrum = chronic venous insufficiency (CEAP classification C0–C6).
ThrombosisVirchow's triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability) → DVT → PE, post-thrombotic syndrome.

los.text: Describe the signs and symptoms of venous disease
los.html:
Varicose veins
  • Dilated, tortuous superficial veins (≥3 mm) in standing patient (great saphenous: medial leg; small saphenous: posterior calf)
  • Symptoms: aching, heaviness, itching, throbbing, swelling, cramps (worse end of day/standing, better with elevation), cosmetic concern
  • Complications: superficial thrombophlebitis (tender red cord), bleeding (minor trauma to thin-walled varix), skin changes, ulceration.
Chronic venous insufficiency/skin changes (CEAP)
  • C1 telangiectasia/reticular veins
  • C2 varicose veins
  • C3 oedema
  • C4 skin changes (haemosiderin pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis (woody induration, "inverted champagne bottle" leg), atrophie blanche)
  • C5 healed ulcer
  • C6 active venous ulcer (shallow, irregular, sloughy, moderately painful, gaiter area (medial malleolus), exudative, with surrounding skin changes, palpable pulses).
DVTUnilateral calf swelling, pain, tenderness, warmth, pitting oedema, dilated superficial veins (Wells score).
Post-thrombotic syndromeChronic pain, swelling, heaviness, skin changes, ulceration after DVT.
Examination
  • Standing inspection
  • Palpation (cough impulse at SFJ, tenderness)
  • Tap test
  • Trendelenburg/tourniquet tests (historical; replaced by duplex)
  • Pulses and ABPI (exclude arterial disease before compression).

los.text: Describe the impact of venous disease on patients
los.html:
PhysicalPain, aching, heaviness, swelling, itching, restricted mobility, leg ulcers (chronic, recurrent: ~70% recur), exudate/odour, infections (cellulitis), bleeding, sleep disturbance.
PsychologicalLow self-esteem, body image concerns (cosmetic), embarrassment (odour, bandages), anxiety, depression, frustration with slow healing.
Social/functional
  • Reduced mobility and activities
  • Social isolation
  • Difficulty with footwear/clothing
  • Time off work
  • Reduced work capacity (occupations requiring standing)
  • Frequent nurse visits for dressings/compression.
EconomicNHS cost (venous ulcers consume a large share of community nursing time; ~£ billions/year for wound care), personal costs.
  • Quality of life significantly reduced (comparable to other chronic diseases), especially in elderly with ulcers
  • Also risk of DVT/PE in active thrombotic disease.

los.text: Describe the surgical and conservative management of venous disease
los.html:
Conservative
  • Leg elevation
  • Exercise/walking (calf pump)
  • Weight loss
  • Avoid prolonged standing
  • Skin care (emollients, topical steroids for venous eczema)
  • Compression (hosiery class 1–3 or bandaging) for symptoms/oedema/ulcers (check ABPI first)
  • Treat infection
  • Analgesia
  • For ulcers: multilayer compression bandaging (see LO 24), wound care, pentoxifylline (aids ulcer healing).
Interventional/surgical (NICE CG168: refer to vascular service if symptomatic varicose veins, skin changes, superficial vein thrombosis with incompetence, bleeding, or active/healed ulcer)
  • Duplex ultrasound to confirm reflux and plan.
  • 1st: endothermal ablation: radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) of incompetent truncal vein under local anaesthetic.
  • 2nd: ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (sodium tetradecyl sulfate).
  • 3rd: open surgery (high ligation and stripping of GSV at saphenofemoral junction; small saphenous ligation at SPJ), phlebectomies (avulsions) for tributaries.
  • Cyanoacrylate glue (non-thermal).
  • Early endovenous ablation in venous ulcers speeds healing and reduces recurrence (EVRA trial).
Deep venous diseaseAnticoagulation (DVT), iliac vein stenting (selected).
Compression hosiery after treatment/for prevention of recurrence (if ABPI adequate).

los.text: Describe how water and solutes permeate capillary walls
los.html:
Capillary structure
  • Single layer of endothelium on basement membrane
  • Types: continuous (muscle, skin, lung, CNS (tight junctions: BBB)), fenestrated (kidney glomeruli, gut, endocrine glands), sinusoidal/discontinuous (liver, spleen, bone marrow: large gaps).
Routes of exchange
  • Lipid-soluble substances (O₂, CO₂, anaesthetics) diffuse directly through endothelial cell membranes (whole surface area; very fast).
  • Water and small water-soluble solutes (glucose, ions, urea) pass through intercellular clefts (gaps between endothelial cells, with glycocalyx as molecular sieve) and fenestrations; water also through aquaporins.
  • Large molecules (proteins): very limited; via vesicular transport (transcytosis/caveolae) and occasional large pores; ↑ in inflammation (endothelial contraction → gaps).
MechanismDriverRole
DiffusionConcentration gradient (Fick: rate ∝ area × gradient × permeability / distance)Main route for solute exchange
Bulk flow/filtrationStarling forcesFluid distribution
  • Endothelial glycocalyx: negatively charged layer restricting protein movement; shedding (sepsis, hyperglycaemia) ↑ leak.

los.text: Describe the role of 'Starling forces' and lymphatic drainage in fluid exchange
los.html:
Starling forces
  • Net filtration = Kf [(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)]:
  • Pc (capillary hydrostatic pressure: ~35 mmHg arteriolar end → ~15 mmHg venular end) pushes fluid out.
  • Pi (interstitial hydrostatic pressure: ~0 or slightly negative).
  • πc (plasma oncotic pressure: ~25 mmHg, mainly albumin) pulls fluid in.
  • πi (interstitial oncotic pressure: small).
  • σ = reflection coefficient (protein permeability: 1 = impermeable).
Classical view
  • Net filtration at the arteriolar end, net reabsorption at the venular end.
  • Revised Starling principle (glycocalyx model): in most tissues there is little venous reabsorption at steady state
  • The oncotic gradient across the glycocalyx limits filtration, and most filtered fluid returns via lymphatics.
Lymphatic drainage
  • Returns ~8 L/day of capillary filtrate to lymph nodes (~4 L reabsorbed there) → ~2–4 L/day to the venous circulation
  • Also returns protein
  • Driven by intrinsic lymphatic contraction, skeletal muscle pump, respiration, valves.
  • Oedema when filtration exceeds lymphatic capacity: ↑ Pc (heart failure, venous hypertension/DVT, fluid overload, CCBs)
  • ↓ πc (hypoalbuminaemia: nephrotic, liver disease, malnutrition)
  • ↑ permeability (inflammation, sepsis, burns)
  • Lymphatic obstruction (lymphoedema: protein-rich, non-pitting late).

los.text: Discuss current theories of venous ulceration.
los.html:
• Venous ulcers develop in skin exposed to sustained venous hypertension (failure of calf pump/valves) in the gaiter area
    • mechanism not fully understood: several theories:
    • Fibrin cuff (Browse & Burnand): fibrinogen leaks → pericapillary fibrin cuffs → block O₂/nutrient diffusion → hypoxia → ulcer. Probably a marker, not the sole cause.
    • White cell trapping (Coleridge Smith): slow capillary flow → leucocytes trapped and activated → enzymes, free radicals, cytokines → endothelial damage → tissue destruction.
    • Growth factor trapping theory (Falanga & Eaglstein): macromolecules (fibrinogen, α2-macroglobulin) leaking into dermis trap growth factors (TGF-β) → unavailable for tissue repair → impaired healing.
    • Microangiopathy/MMP imbalance: ↑ matrix metalloproteinases, ↓ TIMPs → excessive matrix degradation; senescent fibroblasts; iron deposition (haemosiderin → oxidative stress).
    • Mechanical: oedema increases diffusion distance; minor trauma triggers breakdown.
  • Current consensus: venous hypertension → chronic inflammation (leucocyte–endothelial interactions, cytokines, MMPs, iron) → skin changes (lipodermatosclerosis) → ulceration
    • hence compression (reverses venous hypertension) is the cornerstone of treatment.

los.text: Describe microcirculation and the impact diabetes has on the vascular system
los.html:
Microcirculation
  • Arterioles (resistance; sympathetic/local control), capillaries (exchange), venules
  • Regulated by local metabolites (adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, lactate → vasodilation), myogenic response, endothelial factors (NO, prostacyclin vs endothelin), autonomic nerves
  • Precapillary sphincters/arteriovenous shunts (skin thermoregulation).
Diabetes effects on the vascular system
  • Microvascular disease: chronic hyperglycaemia → AGEs, polyol pathway, PKC activation, oxidative stress → basement membrane thickening, pericyte loss, endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO), ↑ permeability, impaired hyperaemic response to injury/inflammation, AV shunting (autonomic neuropathy) → warm, dry foot but poor nutritive capillary flow → retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, impaired wound healing. (No "small vessel occlusive disease" in the sense of blocked arterioles; it is functional.)
  • Macrovascular disease: accelerated atherosclerosis, especially distal (infrapopliteal/tibial) arteries, often bilateral and multisegmental; medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg) → incompressible arteries → falsely high ABPI; poorer collaterals.
  • Neuropathy (sensory: loss of protective sensation; motor: clawing, high pressures; autonomic: dry cracked skin) + ischaemia + infection (impaired neutrophil function) → diabetic foot ulcers, Charcot neuroarthropathy, gangrene, amputation (diabetes is the leading cause of non-traumatic amputation).

los.text: Describe how to assess someone's circulation including ulcers and their differences
los.html:
Circulation assessment
  • History (claudication, rest pain, previous vascular surgery, diabetes, smoking)
  • Inspection (colour, hair loss, shiny skin, nails, ulcers, gangrene, between toes, heels)
  • Temperature
  • Capillary refill (>2 s abnormal)
  • Pulses (femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial; ± bruits)
  • Buerger's test (pallor on elevation, reactive hyperaemia on dependency)
  • Handheld Doppler (triphasic normal → biphasic → monophasic → absent)
  • ABPI, toe pressures/TBPI (diabetes, calcified vessels), duplex.
Ulcer assessment
  • Site
  • Size (measure/photograph)
  • Shape
  • Edge
  • Base
  • Depth (probe to bone → osteomyelitis)
  • Exudate
  • Surrounding skin
  • Pain
  • Infection signs
  • Sensation (10 g monofilament, vibration).
VenousArterialNeuropathic (diabetic)
SiteGaiter area (medial malleolus)Distal: toes, heels, pressure points, lateral malleolus, shinPressure areas: plantar metatarsal heads, heel, toes
AppearanceShallow, irregular sloping edges, sloughy/granulating base, exudativePunched out, deep, regular, pale/necrotic base, little exudatePunched out with callus rim, may be deep
PainMild–moderate (better elevated)Very painful (worse elevated, at night)Painless
Surrounding skinHaemosiderin, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, oedema, varicose veinsCold, pale, shiny, hairless; dependent ruborWarm (if no PAD), dry, cracked, callus; deformity (claw toes, Charcot)
Pulses/ABPIPresent; ABPI normal (≥0.8)Absent/↓; ABPI <0.5–0.8Present (unless mixed); ABPI may be falsely high
  • Mixed ulcers (venous + arterial) common in elderly: modified compression if ABPI 0.5–0.8.

los.text: Describe the role of podiatry
los.html:
PodiatryFoot health specialists; essential in the diabetic foot MDT.
Roles
  • Annual foot screening and risk stratification (low, moderate, high, active) (NICE NG19): sensation (monofilament), pulses, deformity, skin, previous ulcer/amputation.
  • Education: daily foot inspection, footwear, nail care, avoid barefoot walking/heat sources, when to seek help.
  • Preventive care: callus debridement, nail care (ingrown/thickened nails), corns, treating fungal infections.
  • Offloading: total contact casts, removable walkers, therapeutic footwear, insoles/orthotics → redistribute pressure (key to healing neuropathic ulcers).
  • Wound care: sharp debridement, dressings, monitoring healing, recognising infection/ischaemia → urgent referral to multidisciplinary foot care service (within 1 working day for active diabetic foot problems).
  • Charcot foot recognition (hot, swollen foot in neuropathic patient → offload, urgent MDT).
  • Biomechanical assessment, gait analysis, MSK foot problems.
ImpactMDT foot care with podiatry reduces amputations substantially.

los.text: Describe the investigation, management and complications of circulatory diseases
los.html:
Investigations of circulatory disease
  • ABPI
  • Toe pressures
  • Duplex ultrasound (arterial stenosis/occlusion; venous reflux/DVT)
  • CT angiography/MR angiography (planning revascularisation)
  • Digital subtraction angiography (diagnostic + therapeutic)
  • Bloods (FBC, U&E (contrast), lipids, HbA1c, CRP, thrombophilia if young)
  • ECG/echo (embolic source, comorbidity)
  • X-ray/MRI foot (osteomyelitis)
  • Wound swabs/bone biopsy
  • D-dimer + USS (DVT)
  • Ultrasound aorta (AAA).
Management
  • Risk factor modification/best medical therapy (smoking, statin, antiplatelet, BP, glucose, weight, exercise).
  • Arterial: supervised exercise, revascularisation (angioplasty, stenting, bypass, endarterectomy), amputation; acute ischaemia → heparin, embolectomy/thrombolysis.
  • Venous: compression, endovenous ablation/foam/surgery, anticoagulation for DVT.
  • Diabetic foot: offloading, debridement, antibiotics (osteomyelitis: prolonged), revascularisation, glucose control, MDT.
  • Lymphoedema: decongestive therapy (LO 28).
Complications of circulatory diseases
  • Ulceration
  • Gangrene
  • Infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis)
  • Amputation
  • Acute limb ischaemia
  • MI/stroke (systemic atherosclerosis)
  • AAA rupture
  • PE (DVT)
  • Post-thrombotic syndrome
  • Chronic pain
  • Immobility
  • Depression
  • Treatment complications (graft occlusion/infection, contrast nephropathy, bleeding, reperfusion injury, compartment syndrome).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the deep and superficial venous systems
los.html:
Superficial veins(in subcutaneous tissue, above deep fascia)
  • Great (long) saphenous vein (GSV): from medial end of dorsal venous arch → passes anterior to the medial malleolus (venous cut-down site) → up medial leg (with saphenous nerve below knee: injury in stripping) → behind medial femoral condyle → medial thigh → through the saphenous opening (cribriform fascia) ~3–4 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle → saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) with femoral vein in femoral triangle. Tributaries at SFJ (superficial epigastric, circumflex iliac, external pudendal).
  • Small (short) saphenous vein (SSV): from lateral end of dorsal venous arch → posterior to the lateral malleolus (with sural nerve) → up midline of calf → pierces deep fascia → saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ) with popliteal vein in popliteal fossa (variable level).
Deep veins
  • Beneath deep fascia; accompany arteries (paired venae comitantes below the knee).
  • Route: anterior tibial, posterior tibial, fibular veins → popliteal vein → femoral vein (+ profunda femoris vein) → common femoral vein → external iliac vein.
  • Femoral vein lies medial to the artery at the inguinal ligament.
  • Soleal and gastrocnemius sinuses: calf pump; where DVTs start.
Perforating (communicating) veinsConnect superficial → deep through deep fascia (thigh: Hunterian/Dodd; calf: Cockett perforators medial lower leg), valves direct flow superficial → deep.

los.text: Describe NICE guidelines for treatment of venous disease
los.html:
NICE CG168 (Varicose veins: diagnosis and management)
  • Refer to a vascular service people with: symptomatic primary or recurrent varicose veins; lower-limb skin changes (pigmentation, eczema) thought to be due to chronic venous insufficiency; superficial vein thrombosis (hard, painful veins) and suspected venous incompetence; venous leg ulcer (break in skin below knee not healed within 2 weeks); healed venous leg ulcer. Refer bleeding varicose veins immediately.
  • Assessment: duplex ultrasound to confirm diagnosis and extent of truncal reflux and plan treatment.
  • Treatment for confirmed truncal reflux: 1st endothermal ablation (RFA or EVLA); if unsuitable → ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy; if unsuitable → surgery. Treat tributaries at same time or later.
  • Compression hosiery: don't offer to treat varicose veins unless interventional treatment is unsuitable; not routinely after treatment except as adjunct.
  • Pregnancy: don't offer interventional treatment (consider compression for symptoms).
  • Information on what varicose veins are, likely progression, lifestyle (exercise, weight, elevation, avoid prolonged standing).
NICE CKS venous leg ulcer
  • Assess ABPI
  • Full compression (40 mmHg) if ABPI ≥0.8
  • Refer to vascular service for endovenous treatment (EVRA evidence)
  • Refer if not healed in 2 weeks or ABPI <0.8 / >1.3.

los.text: Describe the basic principles of treatments for venous disease - triple layer compression
los.html:
Aim
  • Counteract venous hypertension
  • → ↑ venous return, ↓ venous pressure and reflux, ↓ oedema (↑ interstitial pressure), improve microcirculation and calf pump efficiency
  • → heals venous ulcers (~60–70% at 12 weeks) and prevents recurrence.
Graduated compressionHighest at ankle, decreasing up the leg (Laplace: pressure ∝ tension / radius → leg naturally wider proximally).
  • Multilayer bandaging (3- or 4-layer) for active ulcers
  • Applied by trained nurse: e.g. (1) orthopaedic wool padding (protects bony prominences, reshapes limb)
  • (2) crepe (smooths)
  • (3) light compression/elastic bandage
  • (4) cohesive outer layer (holds in place)
  • Delivers ~40 mmHg at ankle
  • Changed weekly (more often if exudative)
  • Short-stretch (inelastic) bandages are an alternative (high working pressure, low resting pressure).
  • Compression wraps and ulcer hosiery kits are newer options.
Before compression: ABPI essential
  • ≥0.8: full compression safe.
  • 0.5–0.8: reduced (modified) compression under specialist supervision (mixed disease).
  • <0.5: no compression (critical ischaemia; risk of pressure necrosis/amputation) → vascular referral.
  • >1.3 (calcified): unreliable → toe pressures/duplex.
Contraindications/cautionsSignificant PAD, uncontrolled heart failure, severe peripheral neuropathy, fragile skin, allergies.
After healingClass 2–3 compression hosiery lifelong to prevent recurrence; skin care; exercise.

los.text: Describe the lymphatic function, drainage, anatomy, physiology
los.html:
Function
  • Return of interstitial fluid and protein to blood (prevents oedema; maintains plasma volume)
  • Immune surveillance (antigen/dendritic cell transport to nodes)
  • Absorption of dietary fat (lacteals → chylomicrons)
  • Removal of debris/microbes.
Anatomy
  • Blind-ended initial lymphatics (overlapping endothelial flaps, anchoring filaments open them when interstitial pressure rises)
  • → pre-collectors
  • → collecting lymphatics (smooth muscle, valves; segments = lymphangions that contract rhythmically)
  • → lymph nodes
  • → trunks
  • → thoracic duct (from cisterna chyli at L1–L2; drains lower body, left upper body; empties into left venous angle (left IJV/subclavian junction)) and right lymphatic duct (right upper body).
Lower limb drainage
  • Superficial lymphatics follow great saphenous vein → superficial inguinal nodes
  • Deep lymphatics follow deep veins → popliteal nodes → deep inguinal nodes → external iliac nodes.
Physiology
  • Lymph formation driven by Starling filtration
  • Propulsion by intrinsic contraction, skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pressure changes, arterial pulsation
  • Flow ~2–4 L/day to blood.
  • Lymphoedema when lymphatic transport capacity falls below the lymphatic load.

los.text: Describe the different types of lymphoedema
los.html:
Primary lymphoedema(developmental abnormality of lymphatics; genetic)
  • Congenital (at birth, <2 yrs): Milroy disease (VEGFR3/FLT4 mutation); syndromic: Turner syndrome, Noonan.
  • Praecox (puberty to 35; commonest primary; often female, lower limbs): Meige disease; lymphoedema–distichiasis (FOXC2).
  • Tarda (>35 yrs).
Secondary lymphoedema(acquired; much more common)
  • Cancer treatment: lymph node dissection (axillary → arm after breast cancer; inguinal/pelvic → leg after gynaecological, prostate, melanoma), radiotherapy.
  • Malignant infiltration/obstruction of lymphatics (recurrent cancer, lymphoma).
  • Infection: filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti: commonest cause worldwide; "elephantiasis"), recurrent cellulitis (damages lymphatics and is a complication), TB.
  • Venous disease (phlebolymphoedema), obesity (obesity-related lymphoedema), immobility/dependency ("chair-bound" legs), trauma/surgery (vein harvesting), podoconiosis (silica soil, barefoot).
Lipoedema(differential)Symmetrical fat deposition in legs (women), sparing feet, painful/bruising, not true lymphoedema.

los.text: Describe the presentation, investigation and management of lymphoedema
los.html:
Presentation
  • Gradual swelling of limb (distal to proximal; may include hand/foot dorsum), heaviness/tightness, aching, ↓ mobility
  • Initially pitting, later non-pitting (fibrosis, fat deposition)
  • Stemmer's sign (can't pinch skin at base of 2nd toe/finger: positive in lymphoedema)
  • Skin changes: thickening, hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis ("cobblestone"), deepened skin folds, lymphorrhoea (leakage), recurrent cellulitis
  • Psychological impact and body image.
  • Stages (ISL 0–III).
Investigations
  • Mainly clinical
  • Measure limb volume (circumferential measurements/perometry)
  • Exclude other causes: bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, albumin, TFTs, BNP), duplex (DVT/venous disease), ABPI (before compression)
  • Lymphoscintigraphy (gold standard to confirm lymphatic dysfunction), CT/MRI (exclude malignant obstruction: pelvic/abdominal masses), genetic testing (primary), filarial testing (travel).
  • Unexplained unilateral swelling → exclude cancer.
Management(lymphoedema specialist service, lifelong)
  • See LO 28
  • Plus prompt treatment of cellulitis (antibiotics; prophylactic penicillin if recurrent ≥2/yr), weight management, skin care, exercise, psychological support
  • Avoid diuretics (ineffective unless other cause).

los.text: Describe the basic principles of treatments for lymphoedema
los.html:
Decongestive lymphatic therapy (DLT/complex decongestive therapy)
  • Two phases:
  • Intensive phase: multilayer lymphoedema bandaging (MLLB: short-stretch, ~2–4 weeks) to reduce volume, manual lymphatic drainage (MLD) (specialised gentle massage redirecting lymph to functioning lymphatics), skin care, exercise.
  • Maintenance phase: compression garments (made-to-measure/flat-knit, worn daily), self-lymphatic drainage, exercise, skin care.
The 4 cornerstonesSkin care (emollients, prevent breaks, treat fungal infection: reduce cellulitis), compression, exercise/movement (activates muscle pump, lymphatic contraction), lymphatic drainage (MLD/SLD).
OtherIntermittent pneumatic compression (adjunct), kinesiotaping, weight loss, elevation; cellulitis prevention and management (BLS/Lymphoedema Support Network guidelines).
Surgery(selected, refractory)Lymphaticovenous anastomosis (LVA), vascularised lymph node transfer, liposuction (for fat-dominant, non-pitting limb) with lifelong compression after; debulking (rare).
Prevention after cancer surgerySentinel node biopsy (vs axillary clearance), early surveillance, exercise, avoid cellulitis.

los.text: Describe the signs and symptoms and link with mechanism of injury and clinical management in an elderly patient with a fractured hip.
los.html:
Typical patientElderly (often female), osteoporotic, fall from standing height (low-energy).
Signs and symptoms
  • Pain in groin/hip (may be referred to knee)
  • Unable to weight-bear (some impacted fractures can walk)
  • Shortened and externally rotated leg (displaced fracture: iliopsoas pulls lesser trochanter; gluteal pull on greater trochanter)
  • Pain on hip rotation/axial loading
  • Bruising (later).
  • Look for cause of fall (syncope, stroke, infection), injuries, long lie (pressure sores, rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, dehydration).
TypeNotesTreatment (NICE CG124)
Intracapsular (femoral neck)
  • Retrograde blood supply (medial circumflex femoral artery via retinacular vessels) disrupted → avascular necrosis, non-union when displaced.
  • Garden classification I–IV (I–II undisplaced, III–IV displaced)
  • Undisplaced: internal fixation (cannulated screws) or hemiarthroplasty if unfit.
  • Displaced: hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement (THR if previously independently mobile, not cognitively impaired, fit)
Extracapsular – intertrochantericBlood supply preservedSliding hip screw (DHS)
Extracapsular – subtrochantericIntramedullary nail
  • Management: analgesia (IV paracetamol, opioids, fascia iliaca block)
    • X-ray (AP pelvis + lateral hip; MRI/CT if occult)
    • bloods (FBC, U&E, G&S, CK)
    • ECG
    • surgery on day of or day after admission
    • VTE prophylaxis
    • orthogeriatric care
    • early mobilisation (day after surgery)
    • delirium prevention
    • nutrition
    • bone health (DEXA not needed to start: bisphosphonate after vitamin D repletion)
    • falls assessment
    • rehabilitation. ~30-day mortality ~6–7%
    • 1-year ~25–30%.

los.text: Describe the common causes of falls in the elderly and link to likely outcomes and preventative strategies.
los.html:
Causes (usually multifactorial)
  • Intrinsic: gait and balance problems, muscle weakness/sarcopenia, visual impairment (cataract, bifocals), postural hypotension, cognitive impairment/dementia, delirium, neurological (Parkinson's, stroke, neuropathy), arthritis/foot problems, urinary incontinence/nocturia (rushing to toilet), cardiac (arrhythmias, syncope, aortic stenosis), hypoglycaemia, fear of falling, frailty.
  • Medications (polypharmacy): sedatives/hypnotics (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs), antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, diuretics, opioids, anticholinergics, hypoglycaemics.
  • Extrinsic/environmental: poor lighting, loose rugs/clutter, stairs, slippery floors, inappropriate footwear, lack of grab rails, pets.
  • Situational: alcohol, rushing, acute illness (infection).
Outcomes
  • Fractures (hip, wrist, vertebral, pelvis, humerus), head injury/subdural (anticoagulated), long lie (rhabdomyolysis, pressure ulcers, hypothermia, pneumonia, dehydration), loss of confidence/fear of falling
  • → reduced activity
  • → deconditioning
  • → more falls, loss of independence, care home admission, death (falls are a leading cause of injury death in >75s).
Prevention (NICE/World Falls Guidelines 2022)Multifactorial risk assessment for anyone with ≥1 injurious fall, ≥2 falls, or gait/balance problems.
InterventionDetail
Strength and balance exerciseOtago, FaME: strongest evidence
Medication reviewDeprescribe fall-risk drugs
Home hazardsOT assessment and modification
VisionCataract surgery, single-lens glasses outdoors
CardiovascularTreat postural hypotension; assess syncope
OtherContinence, footwear/podiatry, vitamin D, bone protection, hip protectors (care homes), telecare alarms, education

los.text: Describe the evidence base underlying the epidemiology and prevention of hip fractures.
los.html:
Epidemiology of hip fractures (UK)
  • ~70,000–75,000 per year
  • Mean age ~83
  • ~75% women
  • Incidence rises exponentially with age
  • Numbers increasing with ageing population
  • Cost >£1–2 billion/year
  • ~25–30% 1-year mortality
  • Many lose independence (~25% move to higher-level care).
Risk factors
  • Osteoporosis (age, female, low BMI, previous fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol >3 units/day, glucocorticoids, RA, secondary causes)
  • Falls (see LO 30)
  • Frailty
  • Dementia
  • Care home residence
  • Vitamin D deficiency
  • Sedative drugs.
Prevention evidence
  • Fracture risk assessment (FRAX, QFracture) ± DEXA (T-score ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis).
  • Bisphosphonates (alendronate, zoledronate): ↓ vertebral (~50–70%) and hip fractures (~40%) in osteoporotic women; denosumab, romosozumab/teriparatide (anabolic) for very high risk; HRT (younger postmenopausal); adequate calcium and vitamin D (reduce hip fracture mainly in deficient/institutionalised elderly).
  • Fracture liaison services (secondary prevention after first fragility fracture: "capture the fracture").
  • Exercise programmes reduce falls (~23%) and probably fractures; multifactorial interventions reduce falls in community.
  • Hip protectors: may reduce hip fractures in care homes (adherence poor), not community.
  • Population: physical activity, smoking cessation, nutrition, alcohol reduction.
National Hip Fracture Database audits care standards (Best Practice Tariff: surgery within 36 h, orthogeriatric review, bone health).

los.text: Identify principles of investigation and link them to treatment of fractures and their complications.
los.html:
Investigation principles
  • History (mechanism, energy, time, comorbidities, anticoagulants)
  • Examination (deformity, swelling, skin integrity (open?), neurovascular status distal, compartments, other injuries: ATLS for high-energy)
  • X-ray: two orthogonal views
  • Include joint above and below
  • Additional views (scaphoid, skyline)
  • CT (complex/intra-articular, pelvis, spine, planning)
  • MRI (occult fractures: scaphoid, hip; soft tissue/ligaments)
  • Bloods (pre-op, bone profile, pathological fracture work-up: myeloma screen, PSA)
  • Bone scan/biopsy (pathological).
Treatment principles (orthopaedic "4 Rs")
  • Resuscitate (ABCDE; life before limb)
  • Reduce (closed manipulation or open reduction if displaced)
  • Restrict/hold (immobilisation: cast, splint, traction, internal fixation (plates, screws, nails) or external fixation)
  • Rehabilitate (physio, OT, early mobilisation).
  • Plus analgesia, tetanus, antibiotics and debridement for open fractures (BOAST: IV antibiotics within 1 h, photograph, saline-soaked dressing, theatre within 12–24 h).
Complications
  • Early: neurovascular injury (e.g. radial nerve with humeral shaft, axillary nerve with shoulder dislocation, brachial artery with supracondylar fracture, popliteal artery with knee dislocation), compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch; fasciotomy), fat embolism (long bones: hypoxia, confusion, petechial rash), haemorrhage/shock (pelvis, femur), infection (open fractures), VTE, skin necrosis/pressure from casts, rhabdomyolysis.
  • Late: malunion, delayed union, non-union, avascular necrosis (scaphoid proximal pole, femoral head, talus), osteomyelitis, post-traumatic arthritis (intra-articular), stiffness, complex regional pain syndrome, growth disturbance (physeal injuries), heterotopic ossification, implant failure.

los.text: Perform a structured clinical examination of the groin and scrotum, systematically assessing for common pathologies
los.html:
PreparationConsent, chaperone, privacy, expose groin and genitalia (patient standing first then lying), warm hands/gloves.
Groin
  • Inspection (standing): swellings in groin/scrotum, scars, asymmetry; ask to cough (expansile impulse).
  • Palpation: locate pubic tubercle and ASIS (inguinal ligament between); hernia: site relative to pubic tubercle (inguinal: above and medial; femoral: below and lateral), cough impulse, reducibility (ask patient to reduce or lie down), whether you can get above it (scrotal swelling: can't get above → inguinal hernia), tenderness (strangulation), contralateral side; deep ring occlusion test (midpoint of inguinal ligament: if hernia controlled on coughing → indirect; unreliable); lymph nodes (inguinal: horizontal and vertical groups), femoral pulse, other masses (saphena varix: thrill on coughing, disappears lying).
Scrotum
  • Inspection: size, skin (erythema, ulceration, sebaceous cysts), position of testes (high-riding horizontal in torsion), swelling.
  • Palpation: each testis (size, consistency, lumps, tenderness), epididymis (posterior), spermatic cord (vas deferens, varicocele: "bag of worms", ↑ standing/Valsalva); for any lump: can you get above it? (if not → inguinal hernia), separate from testis? (epididymal cyst), transilluminates? (hydrocele, cysts), consistency, tenderness.
CompleteAbdominal exam, DRE (ICM Year 2 › Gastrointestinal & liver › LO 8), lymph nodes; thank, allow to dress.

los.text: Perform a structured rectal examination to assess for abnormalities in the rectum and surrounding structures
los.html:
See also ICM Year 2 › Gastrointestinal & liver › LO 5 (DRE technique).
Systematic DRE
  • Consent + chaperone
  • → left lateral with knees to chest
  • → inspect perianal skin (fissures, haemorrhoids, fistula openings, skin tags, warts, prolapse, excoriation, blood)
  • → ask to strain
  • → lubricated gloved index finger, gentle insertion
  • → anal tone (resting and squeeze)
  • → sweep 360° (anterior, lateral, posterior walls) for masses (hard, irregular, ulcerated → carcinoma), tenderness, faecal loading (hard stool → impaction)
  • → anterior: prostate in men (size: normal ~walnut/2 finger-breadths; median sulcus; consistency: smooth, rubbery normal/BPH vs hard, craggy, nodular, obliterated sulcus → carcinoma; boggy, exquisitely tender → prostatitis) or cervix/uterus in women (posterior vaginal wall, pouch of Douglas: masses, tenderness)
  • → withdraw
  • → inspect glove (fresh blood, melaena (black tarry), mucus, pus, stool colour (pale)).
DocumentChaperone, consent, findings (e.g. "normal anal tone, no masses, smooth enlarged prostate with preserved median sulcus, brown stool on glove, no blood").

los.text: Interpret common findings from the groin, scrotum, and rectal examinations (e.g., hernias, masses, tenderness, prostate abnormalities)
los.html:
FindingInterpretation
Groin swelling above and medial to pubic tubercle, cough impulse, extends into scrotum, can't get aboveInguinal hernia (indirect: through deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels; direct: through Hesselbach's triangle, medial, older men)
Swelling below and lateral to pubic tubercle, often irreducible, womenFemoral hernia (high strangulation risk → urgent repair)
Tender, tense, irreducible hernia, red skin, vomitingStrangulated/incarcerated hernia → emergency surgery
Soft swelling disappearing on lying, thrill on cough, medial thighSaphena varix
Lump in testis, hard, painless, can't separate from testisTesticular cancer (until proven otherwise)
Fluctuant, transilluminating, surrounding testis (can't feel testis separately)Hydrocele
Separate cystic lump above/behind testis, transilluminatesEpididymal cyst/spermatocele
"Bag of worms" in cord, usually left, ↑ standingVaricocele (new right-sided/non-reducing → renal mass)
Tender swollen epididymis ± testis, fever, dysuriaEpididymo-orchitis
Acutely painful, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflexTesticular torsion (emergency)
Smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery prostateBPH
Hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate, loss of sulcusProstate cancer
Exquisitely tender, boggy prostate, feverAcute prostatitis
Rectal mass, blood on gloveRectal carcinoma, polyp
Tender rectal wall / pelvic tendernessPelvic abscess, appendicitis (pelvic)
Hard stool filling rectumFaecal impaction
Reduced anal tone + saddle anaesthesiaCauda equina syndrome

los.text: Formulate differential diagnoses based on the findings from the groin, scrotum, and rectal examinations, integrating clinical history and presentation
los.html:
Integrate history + findings → differentials
  • Groin lump: hernias (inguinal, femoral), lymphadenopathy (infection: STI, leg; malignancy: lymphoma, melanoma, anal/vulval/penile SCC), saphena varix, femoral artery aneurysm (pulsatile, expansile; post-angiography pseudoaneurysm), lipoma, undescended/ectopic testis, psoas abscess, hydrocele of the cord.
  • Scrotal swelling: painless (hydrocele, epididymal cyst, varicocele, tumour, inguinoscrotal hernia) vs painful (torsion, epididymo-orchitis, trauma/haematocele, torted appendage, Fournier's gangrene (necrotising: diabetic, emergency), mumps orchitis).
  • Rectal findings: bleeding (haemorrhoids, fissure, cancer, IBD, diverticular), pain (fissure, thrombosed haemorrhoid, abscess), change in habit (cancer, IBS, constipation), prostatic symptoms (BPH, cancer, prostatitis).
Weigh with history
  • Age (testicular cancer 15–40; prostate cancer older)
  • Onset (sudden pain → torsion)
  • Sexual history (STI)
  • Systemic symptoms
  • Red flags (weight loss, haematuria, change in bowel habit).
Plan
  • Imaging (scrotal USS for testicular lumps; groin USS for uncertain hernias; CT)
  • Bloods (tumour markers AFP/β-hCG/LDH; PSA; FBC)
  • Urine (MSU, NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea)
  • Referral (2WW urology for testicular mass or suspicious prostate; surgical for hernia; emergency for torsion/strangulation).

los.text: Demonstrate a structured cardiovascular examination, identifying key signs and distinguishing between normal and abnormal findings
los.html:
PreparationWIPER; patient at 45°; chest exposed (dignity); ask about pain.
General inspectionComfortable/breathless, colour (pallor, cyanosis), body habitus (Marfan's), scars, oedema, around bed (GTN spray, O₂, ECG monitoring, fluid restriction chart).
HandsTemperature, CRT, clubbing (endocarditis, cyanotic CHD), splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes, tar staining, xanthomata, peripheral cyanosis.
Pulse
  • Radial (rate, rhythm)
  • Radio-radial and radio-femoral delay (coarctation)
  • Collapsing pulse (AR: raise arm)
  • Brachial/carotid for character and volume (slow-rising: AS; bounding; thready)
  • BP (both arms; postural if indicated).
Face/neck
  • Conjunctival pallor
  • Corneal arcus
  • Xanthelasma
  • Malar flush (MS)
  • Central cyanosis
  • Dental hygiene (endocarditis)
  • JVP (height above sternal angle (normal ≤3–4 cm) and waveform; hepatojugular reflux)
  • Carotid pulse.
Precordium
  • Inspection: scars (median sternotomy: CABG/valve; left thoracotomy: mitral valvotomy; pacemaker/ICD box; saphenous vein harvest scars on legs), visible pulsations, deformity.
  • Palpation: apex beat (normally 5th ICS mid-clavicular line; displaced = LV dilatation; heaving = pressure overload (AS/HTN); thrusting = volume overload), heaves (parasternal: RVH), thrills (palpable murmurs).
  • Auscultation: 4 areas (aortic: 2nd right ICS; pulmonary: 2nd left ICS; tricuspid: 4th/5th left sternal edge; mitral: apex) with diaphragm and bell; time against carotid pulse; manoeuvres: left lateral + bell at apex in expiration (MS), sitting forward in expiration at left sternal edge (AR); radiation to carotids (AS) and axilla (MR).
Back/legsLung bases (crackles, effusion), sacral oedema, ankle oedema, peripheral pulses.
Complete"I would like to check observations, perform ECG, urine dipstick (haematuria: endocarditis), fundoscopy (hypertensive/diabetic retinopathy, Roth spots)."

los.text: Summarise and present cardiovascular examination findings clearly, concisely, and using appropriate medical terminology
los.html:
Template
  • "I examined Mr X, a 72-year-old man, who was comfortable at rest/breathless on minimal exertion.
  • Peripherally: [pulse rate, regular/irregular, character], BP, [no] clubbing or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, JVP raised at x cm.
  • Precordium: [scars], apex beat [undisplaced/displaced to 6th ICS anterior axillary line], [heaving/thrusting], [no] heaves or thrills.
  • Heart sounds: S1 and S2 present, [soft S2/added S3], with a [grade 3/6] ejection systolic murmur loudest in the aortic area radiating to the carotids.
  • Lung bases: [fine bibasal crackles], [pitting oedema to mid-shins]."
Summary"These findings are consistent with aortic stenosis (likely severe given slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and soft S2), with signs of congestive cardiac failure."
Murmur descriptionTiming (systolic/diastolic; early/mid/late/pan), site where loudest, radiation, grade (1–6; ≥4 thrill), character/pitch, relation to respiration and position.
Include pertinent negatives (e.g. no signs of endocarditis, heart failure, or anticoagulation-related bruising with a mechanical valve: "crisp metallic S2").

los.text: Apply clinical reasoning and synthesize differential diagnoses using findings from the cardiovascular examination and propose further investigations
los.html:
• Reasoning from signs:
SignsLikely diagnosisInvestigations
Ejection systolic murmur → carotids, slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressureAortic stenosisEcho (valve area, gradient), ECG (LVH), CT/angio pre-TAVI
Pansystolic murmur at apex → axilla, displaced apex, AFMitral regurgitationEcho, ECG
Early diastolic murmur LSE, collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressureAortic regurgitationEcho, CT aorta (root dilatation)
Mid-diastolic murmur at apex, malar flush, AF, tapping apexMitral stenosisEcho
↑ JVP, bibasal crackles, oedema, S3, displaced apexHeart failureNT-proBNP, echo, ECG, CXR, bloods
Fever + new murmur ± splinters, Osler's, JanewayInfective endocarditis3 blood cultures, TTE/TOE, CRP
Irregularly irregular pulseAFECG, TFTs, echo, CHA₂DS₂-VASc
Radio-femoral delay, HTN in youngCoarctationEcho, CT/MR aorta
↑ JVP with Kussmaul's sign, pulsus paradoxus, muffled sounds, hypotensionTamponade/constrictionUrgent echo
Midline sternotomy + metallic clickProsthetic valveINR, echo
  • General: ECG, CXR, bloods (FBC, U&E, TFT, lipids, HbA1c, troponin if acute), echocardiogram for any significant murmur; refer cardiology.

los.text: Demonstrate a systematic and thorough peripheral vascular examination, identifying normal and abnormal findings
los.html:
PreparationWIPER; patient lying flat/at 45°, legs exposed (dignity); ask about pain.
General inspectionAmputations, scars (bypass grafts, angioplasty sites in groin), colour, posture (leg hanging over bed: rest pain), around bed (walking aids, dressings).
Hands/arms
  • Temperature
  • CRT
  • Tar staining
  • Xanthomata
  • Radial pulses (rate, rhythm: AF → embolic)
  • Radio-radial delay
  • BP in both arms (subclavian stenosis: >20 mmHg difference).
NeckCarotid bruits (auscultate).
AbdomenPalpate for AAA (expansile pulsatile mass above umbilicus: two fingers move apart), auscultate for aortic/renal bruits.
Legs
  • Inspection: colour (pallor, cyanosis, dependent rubor), hair loss, shiny atrophic skin, nail changes, ulcers (check between toes and heels), gangrene, muscle wasting, scars, varicose veins, venous skin changes.
  • Palpation: temperature (back of hands, compare sides), capillary refill (toe pulp >2 s), pulses: femoral (mid-inguinal point), popliteal (knee flexed ~30°, both hands, deep in fossa), posterior tibial (behind medial malleolus), dorsalis pedis (lateral to EHL tendon); ± femoral bruits; palpate for popliteal aneurysm (easily felt, prominent pulse).
  • Buerger's test: elevate legs (pallor at angle <20° = severe ischaemia: Buerger's angle), then hang over side → reactive hyperaemia/rubor (positive).
  • Sensation (neuropathy: monofilament).
CompleteABPI and handheld Doppler, neurological exam of legs, cardiovascular exam, full venous exam if indicated.
InterpretAbsent pulses below a level localise disease (e.g. absent popliteal + distal = femoropopliteal disease); weak/absent femoral = aorto-iliac.

los.text: Measure and interpret Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) to assess peripheral arterial disease
los.html:
ABPI (ankle–brachial pressure index)Highest ankle systolic pressure (DP or PT) ÷ highest brachial systolic pressure (of both arms), measured for each leg.
Technique
  • Patient supine, rested 10–20 min
  • Appropriately sized BP cuff
  • Handheld Doppler (8 MHz) with gel: brachial pulses (both arms: use higher), then ankle cuff above malleoli
  • → dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial signals
  • → inflate until signal disappears, deflate slowly
  • → pressure at which signal returns = systolic
  • Calculate for each leg.
ABPIInterpretation
>1.3–1.4Incompressible, calcified arteries (diabetes, CKD, elderly) → unreliable: use toe pressures/TBPI, duplex
1.0–1.3 (0.9–1.3)Normal
0.8–0.9Mild PAD
0.5–0.8Moderate PAD (claudication); compression only under specialist guidance
<0.5Severe/critical ischaemia (rest pain, tissue loss): urgent vascular referral; no compression
  • Uses: diagnosis of PAD (<0.9), severity, safety check before compression bandaging (≥0.8 full compression), monitoring after revascularisation
    • low ABPI also predicts CV events.
  • Exercise ABPI (drop after treadmill) if resting normal but symptoms of claudication.

los.text: Identify common fractures and dislocations on plain radiographs, including typical injury patterns (e.g., Colles’, boxer’s, femoral neck, scaphoid, greenstick)
los.html:
FractureMechanism/patientX-ray appearance
Colles'FOOSH, older woman (osteoporosis)Distal radius fracture (~2.5 cm from wrist) with dorsal displacement/angulation ("dinner fork"), ± ulnar styloid fracture
Smith'sFall on flexed wristDistal radius with volar displacement
ScaphoidFOOSH, young adultWaist fracture (may be occult: scaphoid series; MRI if suspected)
Boxer'sPunching5th metacarpal neck with volar angulation of head
Femoral neckElderly fallIntracapsular: disruption of Shenton's line, trabecular pattern, shortening; Garden classification; extracapsular (intertrochanteric)
GreenstickChildren (soft, bendy bone)Incomplete fracture: one cortex breaks, other bends (convex side)
Buckle (torus)Children, FOOSHBulging of cortex (compression), distal radius
Supracondylar humerusChildren, FOOSH on extended elbowPosterior displacement; anterior humeral line doesn't intersect capitellum middle third; posterior fat pad sign; brachial artery/median nerve risk
Ankle (Weber A/B/C)Inversion/eversionFibular fracture level relative to syndesmosis (C above → unstable)
Shoulder dislocationSee LO 46
Vertebral compressionOsteoporosisLoss of height (wedge)
  • Ottawa rules for ankle/knee X-ray decisions.

los.text: Distinguish between normal variants (e.g., unfused epiphyses, accessory ossicles, sesamoid bones, bipartite patella) and true fractures
los.html:
Normal variantFeatureMimics
Unfused epiphyses/growth plates (physes)Smooth, regular lucent lines in predictable locations, symmetrical (compare with other side), sclerotic marginsFractures (Salter–Harris injuries involve physis)
Secondary ossification centres/apophysesPredictable timing (e.g. elbow CRITOE: Capitellum 1, Radial head 3, Internal (medial) epicondyle 5, Trochlea 7, Olecranon 9, External (lateral) epicondyle 11 years)Avulsion fragments (trochlea before medial epicondyle = displaced medial epicondyle)
Accessory ossiclesSmooth, well-corticated round/oval bones (os trigonum (behind talus), os naviculare, os peroneum, os acromiale)Avulsion fractures (which are irregular, non-corticated on the fracture side, acute)
Sesamoid bonesCorticated, within tendons (patella, 1st MTP sesamoids, thumb)Fractures
Bipartite patellaSuperolateral fragment with smooth corticated margins, often bilateralPatellar fracture (sharp, non-corticated edges, usually transverse)
Nutrient foramina/vascular channelsThin oblique lucency through one cortexFracture lines
Mach bands, overlapping soft tissue/skin foldsEdge-enhancement artefactFracture/pneumothorax
  • Clues for true fracture: sharp, non-corticated lucent line, cortical breach/step, displacement, soft-tissue swelling, clinical tenderness at that site
    • compare with the contralateral side or reference atlas when unsure.

los.text: Describe the radiographic features of fractures, including fracture line, comminution, impaction, displacement, angulation, and intra-articular extension
los.html:
Fracture line
  • Transverse (perpendicular to long axis: direct blow/bending), oblique (angled), spiral (twisting; in non-ambulant children → consider NAI), longitudinal
  • Complete vs incomplete (greenstick, buckle, bowing).
Comminution>2 fragments (high energy, osteoporosis); segmental (two separate fracture lines isolating a segment); butterfly fragment.
ImpactionFragments driven into each other (increased density/sclerotic band, shortening): impacted femoral neck, distal radius, humeral neck.
Displacement (translation)Distal fragment's position relative to proximal, as % of bone width (e.g. "50% dorsal displacement").
AngulationDirection the apex points or direction of distal fragment tilt (state convention: e.g. "dorsal angulation of distal fragment" / "apex volar"), in degrees.
RotationClinically (scissoring fingers) or on X-ray (different widths of fragments).
Shortening/distractionOverlap or gap between fragments.
Intra-articular extensionFracture enters joint surface → step (articular incongruity) → risk of post-traumatic OA → often needs anatomical reduction (ORIF).
Other descriptors
  • Avulsion (ligament/tendon pulls fragment)
  • Compression/crush (vertebrae)
  • Pathological (through lesion: lytic metastasis, cyst)
  • Stress (periosteal reaction)
  • Open (clinical)
  • Physeal (Salter–Harris I–V: Straight across, Above, Lower (below), Through, Rammed).

los.text: Recognise indirect signs of fracture such as soft tissue swelling, joint effusion, fat pad sign, and lipohaemarthrosis
los.html:
• Soft tissue swelling over the injury site.
  • Joint effusion (fluid distending capsule): e.g. suprapatellar effusion on lateral knee X-ray.
  • Fat pad sign (elbow): on lateral elbow X-ray (90° flexion), anterior fat pad displaced upwards ("sail sign") and/or visible posterior fat pad (normally hidden in olecranon fossa)
    • → joint effusion
    • → occult fracture likely (radial head in adults; supracondylar in children) even if no fracture line seen
    • → treat as fracture (sling, review).
  • Lipohaemarthrosis: fat–fluid level on horizontal-beam lateral X-ray of the knee (fat from bone marrow floats on blood)
    • → intra-articular fracture (e.g. tibial plateau)
    • → CT.
  • Pronator quadratus fat pad displacement (distal forearm fracture)
    • scaphoid fat stripe obliteration
    • sinus tarsi/navicular fat stripe changes
    • pre-vertebral soft tissue swelling (cervical spine injury)
    • pneumothorax/surgical emphysema with rib fractures.
  • Cortical buckling, sclerotic bands (impaction), periosteal reaction (healing/stress fractures, days–weeks later).
  • Action: if indirect signs present but no fracture → treat as fracture, consider further views/CT/MRI or repeat X-ray in 10–14 days.

los.text: Interpret dislocations and subluxations on radiographs, including anterior and posterior shoulder dislocations, elbow, ankle, and acromioclavicular joint dislocations
los.html:
InjuryX-ray findings
Anterior shoulder dislocation (~95%)
  • AP: humeral head lies inferior and medial to the glenoid (below coracoid)
  • Y-view/axillary: head anterior to glenoid.
  • Associated: Hill–Sachs lesion (posterolateral humeral head impaction), bony Bankart (anteroinferior glenoid rim fracture), greater tuberosity fracture
Posterior shoulder dislocation
  • AP can look nearly normal: "light bulb" sign (internally rotated humeral head symmetrical), widened glenohumeral joint space (>6 mm: "rim sign"), loss of half-moon overlap
  • Axillary/Y-view confirms (head posterior)
  • Reverse Hill–Sachs
  • Causes: seizures, electrocution
Elbow dislocation
  • Usually posterior/posterolateral displacement of radius and ulna relative to humerus
  • Check for associated radial head/coronoid fractures ("terrible triad"), neurovascular injury (brachial artery, median/ulnar nerves)
Ankle dislocation/fracture-dislocation
  • Talus displaced from mortise (talar shift: widened medial clear space >4 mm), with malleolar fractures (bimalleolar/trimalleolar)
  • Reduce urgently (skin and NV compromise)
ACJ dislocationElevation of lateral clavicle relative to acromion; ↑ coracoclavicular distance (>13 mm or >50% vs other side); grading (Rockwood I–VI)
SubluxationPartial loss of joint congruity (e.g. AC joint grade II, radial head subluxation "pulled elbow" in children: X-ray usually normal)
  • Always obtain two orthogonal views; post-reduction X-rays; document neurovascular status before and after.

los.text: Explain the potential clinical consequences of fractures and dislocations (e.g., pneumothorax with rib fracture, avascular necrosis of scaphoid, complications of hip fractures)
los.html:
InjuryPotential consequence
Rib fracturesPneumothorax, haemothorax, pulmonary contusion, flail chest, pneumonia (pain → poor ventilation), liver/spleen injury (lower ribs), great vessel injury (1st/2nd rib: high energy)
Scaphoid fractureAvascular necrosis of proximal pole (retrograde blood supply from distal pole via dorsal carpal branch of radial artery), non-union, SNAC wrist (OA)
Femoral neck (intracapsular) fractureAVN of femoral head, non-union; in elderly: delirium, pneumonia, pressure sores, VTE, death (~30% at 1 year), loss of independence
Pelvic fracture
  • Massive haemorrhage (venous plexus, internal iliac branches) → shock
  • Bladder/urethral injury (blood at meatus: don't catheterise), rectal/vaginal injury, sacral plexus injury
Femoral shaft fractureBlood loss ~1–1.5 L, fat embolism, compartment syndrome
Tibial fractureCompartment syndrome, open fractures (subcutaneous bone), non-union
Supracondylar humerus (child)Brachial artery injury → Volkmann's ischaemic contracture; median/AIN nerve injury
Humeral shaftRadial nerve palsy (wrist drop)
Shoulder dislocationAxillary nerve injury, rotator cuff tear (elderly), recurrent instability
Knee dislocationPopliteal artery injury (CTA), common peroneal nerve
Vertebral fracturesSpinal cord injury, instability; osteoporotic: kyphosis, pain
Talus/femoral head/proximal humerusAVN
Intra-articular fracturesPost-traumatic OA
Skull fracturesExtradural haematoma (temporal: MMA), CSF leak, meningitis

los.text: Apply a systematic approach to fracture description, including site, type, alignment, and associated injuries
los.html:
• Systematic description:
1Patient details, view(s) and date, side, adequacy (two views; joint above and below).
2Bone involved and site (diaphysis/metaphysis/epiphysis; proximal/middle/distal third; intra-/extra-articular; named landmarks).
3. Type/patternComplete/incomplete; transverse/oblique/spiral/comminuted/segmental/avulsion/impacted; open/closed (clinical); pathological?
4. AlignmentDisplacement (direction, %), angulation (direction, degrees), rotation, shortening.
5. Joint involvementIntra-articular extension, articular step, dislocation/subluxation.
6. Associated injuriesOther fractures (e.g. ulnar styloid with distal radius; fibula with tibia), soft tissue signs (effusion, gas: open fracture/gas gangrene), foreign bodies.
7. Bone qualityOsteopenia, lytic/sclerotic lesions.
8Compare with previous films.
  • Example (right wrist, AP and lateral):
ElementDescription
FractureTransverse, extra-articular, distal radial metaphysis, ~2 cm from articular surface
AlignmentDorsal displacement and 20° dorsal angulation of the distal fragment
AssociatedUlnar styloid fracture
ConclusionIn keeping with a Colles' fracture

los.text: Evaluate when fracture or dislocation findings represent urgent or life-threatening problems requiring immediate intervention
los.html:
Urgent/life- or limb-threatening
  • Open fractures (bone exposed/wound communicating): IV antibiotics within 1 h, photograph, saline dressing, splint, tetanus, debridement in theatre (BOAST 4).
  • Neurovascular compromise (pulseless/cold limb, absent distal pulses): immediate reduction/realignment, vascular imaging and repair (e.g. knee dislocation, supracondylar fracture with pulseless hand, ankle fracture-dislocation with skin tenting).
  • Compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment): fasciotomy (pulses can remain present).
  • Pelvic fractures with haemodynamic instability: pelvic binder, major haemorrhage protocol, angioembolisation/packing.
  • Femoral shaft fractures: traction splint, blood loss.
  • Spinal fractures with neurological deficit/instability: immobilisation, urgent spinal surgery.
  • Dislocations (especially hip: AVN risk → reduce within 6 h; ankle; elbow): urgent reduction.
  • Skin threatened by displaced fragments (tenting/blanching).
  • Rib fractures with pneumothorax/flail chest; skull fractures with intracranial bleed.
  • Hip fractures in elderly: surgery within 36 h (not immediate, but time-critical).
  • Suspected non-accidental injury (children): safeguarding.
ActionABCDE/ATLS, analgesia, immobilisation, urgent orthopaedic (± vascular/neurosurgical) referral, document NV status.

los.text: Identify and side the femur, describing key features on bones and radiographs.
los.html:
FemurLongest, strongest bone.
Proximal
  • Head (with fovea capitis for ligamentum teres; articulates with acetabulum)
  • Neck (angle ~125° with shaft; anteverted ~10–15°)
  • Greater trochanter (lateral; gluteus medius/minimus, piriformis insert)
  • Lesser trochanter (posteromedial; iliopsoas inserts)
  • Intertrochanteric line (anterior; capsule attachment) and crest (posterior; quadrate tubercle)
  • Trochanteric fossa.
Shaft
  • Anteriorly bowed
  • Linea aspera (posterior ridge; attachments of adductors, vastus medialis/lateralis, short head of biceps), gluteal tuberosity, spiral line, pectineal line.
DistalMedial and lateral condyles (articulate with tibia), epicondyles (collateral ligaments), adductor tubercle (adductor magnus), intercondylar fossa (cruciates), patellar surface (anterior).
Siding
  • Head points medially, the linea aspera is posterior, the patellar surface is anterior/distal, and the lesser trochanter is posteromedial
  • The medial condyle projects further distally (so shaft angles medially when condyles are level).
Radiographs
  • AP and lateral hip/femur: identify head
  • Neck
  • Trochanters
  • Shenton's line (continuous arc along inferior femoral neck and superior obturator foramen: disrupted in neck fracture/dislocation)
  • Cortices
  • Trabecular pattern
  • Knee condyles.

los.text: Describe what structures may be damaged by a fracture of the femoral neck or dislocation of the hip and explain the functional consequences of these injuries.
los.html:
Femoral neck fracture
  • Blood supply to head: mainly medial circumflex femoral artery (retinacular branches running along the neck under the capsule) + lateral circumflex; small contribution from artery of ligamentum teres (obturator; minimal in adults). Displaced intracapsular fracture tears retinacular vessels → avascular necrosis and non-union.
  • Functional consequences: pain, inability to weight-bear, shortened externally rotated leg, loss of independence; collapse/OA later if AVN.
Hip dislocation
  • Posterior (~90%) (dashboard injury, flexed adducted hip): leg shortened, flexed, adducted, internally rotated; sciatic nerve injury (especially common peroneal division → foot drop), posterior acetabular wall fracture, AVN (reduce within 6 h), damage to femoral head (cartilage).
  • Anterior: leg abducted, externally rotated; femoral nerve, artery and vein at risk.
  • Central (through acetabulum): pelvic organ injury, bleeding.
Other structuresLigamentum teres, capsule and labrum, surrounding muscles (gluteals, short external rotators), obturator nerve (anterior/central), and later post-traumatic OA, heterotopic ossification, VTE.

los.text: Locate and describe the anatomical relationships of the great saphenous vein, fascia lata, iliotibial tract, femoral sheath and its contents (and adjacent femoral nerve), obturator nerve, sciatic nerve, femoral nerve, common peroneal nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal fossa and key vessels within, and identify the main muscles and muscle groups that the nerves supply
los.html:
Great saphenous veinMedial leg/thigh in superficial fascia → saphenous opening → femoral vein in femoral triangle (with saphenous nerve below knee).
Fascia lata
  • Deep fascia enclosing the thigh (thickened laterally as the iliotibial tract)
  • Saphenous opening in it ~3 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle (covered by cribriform fascia).
Iliotibial tract (band)
  • Thick lateral band from iliac crest (receives tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus) → Gerdy's tubercle (lateral tibial condyle)
  • Stabilises hip and knee (lateral knee pain in runners: ITB syndrome).
Femoral sheath
  • Funnel-shaped extension of abdominal fascia (transversalis anteriorly, iliacus fascia posteriorly) below the inguinal ligament containing (lateral → medial): femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymph nodes (Cloquet's node), lymphatics, fat: site of femoral hernia).
  • The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath, laterally (NAVY: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/empty space (canal), lateral to medial).
Obturator nerve(L2–4)
  • Medial border of psoas
  • → pelvic wall
  • → obturator foramen
  • → medial thigh: adductors (adductor longus, brevis, magnus (adductor part), gracilis, obturator externus)
  • Skin of medial thigh.
Sciatic nerve(L4–S3)
  • Greater sciatic foramen below piriformis
  • → gluteal region (midway between greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity)
  • → posterior thigh deep to biceps femoris
  • → divides (usually apex of popliteal fossa) into tibial and common peroneal (fibular).
  • Supplies hamstrings (and adductor magnus hamstring part) then all muscles below the knee.
Femoral nerve(L2–4)Lateral to femoral artery → quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus, iliacus; skin anterior thigh; saphenous nerve (medial leg/foot).
Common peroneal nerveWinds around the neck of fibula (vulnerable), then divides:
BranchMuscles (action)Skin
SuperficialLateral compartment: peroneus longus/brevis (eversion)Dorsum of foot
DeepAnterior compartment: tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL (dorsiflexion)1st web space
Tibial nerve
  • Popliteal fossa → deep posterior calf → behind medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel) → medial and lateral plantar nerves
  • Supplies posterior compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL: plantarflexion, inversion), sole of foot.
Popliteal fossa(diamond)
  • Boundaries: biceps femoris (superolateral), semimembranosus/semitendinosus (superomedial), two heads of gastrocnemius (inferior)
  • Contents (superficial → deep): tibial nerve
  • Popliteal vein
  • Popliteal artery (deepest)
  • Common peroneal nerve (lateral, along biceps)
  • Small saphenous vein
  • Popliteal lymph nodes.

los.text: Describe the anatomical basis (nerve root or peripheral nerve) for loss of movements and reflexes at the knee and ankle resulting from spinal injuries, disc lesions and common peripheral nerve injuries.
los.html:
Movement/reflexNerve rootPeripheral nerve
Hip flexionL1–L2 (L3)Femoral (iliopsoas: lumbar plexus)
Hip adductionL2–L3Obturator
Knee extensionL3–L4Femoral (quadriceps)
Knee flexionL5–S1Sciatic (hamstrings)
Ankle dorsiflexionL4–L5Deep peroneal (tibialis anterior)
Big toe extensionL5Deep peroneal (EHL)
Ankle eversionL5–S1Superficial peroneal
Ankle inversionL4–L5Tibial (tibialis posterior) + deep peroneal (tibialis anterior)
Ankle plantarflexionS1–S2Tibial (gastrocnemius/soleus)
Knee jerkL3–L4Femoral
Ankle jerkS1 (S2)Tibial
Disc lesions(posterolateral prolapse compresses the lower root at that level)
  • L4/5 disc → L5 root: weak big toe extension/dorsiflexion, sensory loss dorsum of foot/1st web space, reflexes usually normal
  • L5/S1 disc → S1 root: weak plantarflexion/eversion, lost ankle jerk, sensory loss lateral foot/sole
  • L3/4 → L4: weak knee extension/inversion, ↓ knee jerk, medial leg sensory loss.
Peripheral nerve injuries
  • Common peroneal (fibular neck fracture, tight cast, leg crossing): foot drop
  • Weak dorsiflexion and eversion
  • Inversion preserved (tibialis posterior: tibial nerve)
  • Sensory loss dorsum of foot
  • Reflexes normal (vs L5 root: inversion also weak)
  • Sciatic (hip dislocation, injections, hip surgery): hamstrings + all below knee, lost ankle jerk
  • Femoral (pelvic surgery, haematoma): weak knee extension, ↓ knee jerk
  • Tibial: weak plantarflexion, sole numbness, ↓ ankle jerk.
Spinal cord injuriesUMN signs below level; conus/cauda equina: LMN, saddle anaesthesia, sphincters.

los.text: Identify the sacral plexus and its branches lying on piriformis.
los.html:
Sacral plexus
  • Formed by lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) + ventral rami S1–S4
  • Lies on the anterior surface of piriformis in the posterior pelvic wall, behind the internal iliac vessels and ureter (deep to parietal pelvic fascia).
Branches(mostly leave through the greater sciatic foramen)
  • Sciatic nerve (L4–S3): largest (LO 55).
  • Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1): above piriformis → gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae (abduction; Trendelenburg gait if injured).
  • Inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2): below piriformis → gluteus maximus (hip extension: difficulty rising from chair/climbing stairs).
  • Pudendal nerve (S2–S4): leaves via greater sciatic foramen, re-enters via lesser sciatic foramen → pudendal canal → perineum (sphincters, sensation).
  • Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3): skin of posterior thigh/buttock.
  • Nerve to piriformis (S1–S2), nerve to obturator internus/superior gemellus (L5–S2), nerve to quadratus femoris/inferior gemellus (L4–S1).
  • Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4): parasympathetic to pelvic viscera, hindgut.
  • Perforating cutaneous nerve, nerves to levator ani/coccygeus (S3–4).
ClinicalCompression by pelvic tumours (sacral plexopathy), piriformis syndrome, injury in pelvic fractures/childbirth.
