los.text: Locate the sciatic nerve, which is the large lateral terminal branch of the sacral plexus, and trace it to the greater sciatic foramen and the gluteal region.
los.html:
Sciatic nerve
  • Largest nerve in the body
  • Terminal branch of the sacral plexus (L4–S3)
  • Two divisions in a common sheath: tibial (anterior divisions) and common peroneal (posterior divisions).
Course
  • Forms on piriformis in the pelvis
  • → leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis (common variant: common peroneal division passes through/above piriformis)
  • → enters gluteal region deep to gluteus maximus, lying on the short external rotators (superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus, quadratus femoris), midway between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter
  • → descends into posterior thigh deep to long head of biceps femoris on adductor magnus
  • → usually divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa into tibial and common peroneal nerves.
Supplies
  • Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris (short head: common peroneal division)), hamstring part of adductor magnus
  • via branches, all muscles below the knee and most skin of leg/foot (except medial: saphenous).
Clinical
  • Safe IM injection site = upper outer quadrant of buttock (or ventrogluteal) to avoid the sciatic nerve
  • Injury in posterior hip dislocation, hip replacement, pelvic fractures
  • Sciatica (root compression L5/S1, not the nerve itself usually)
  • Piriformis syndrome.

los.text: Describe the coccygeal plexus and the muscles it supplies.
los.html:
Coccygeal plexus
  • Small plexus formed by the ventral rami of S4, S5 and the coccygeal nerve (Co1)
  • Lies on the pelvic surface of coccygeus muscle.
Branches
  • Motor: to coccygeus and the posterior part of levator ani (iliococcygeus) (with S4 contributions: nerve to levator ani) → pelvic floor support.
  • Sensory: anococcygeal nerves → pierce the sacrotuberous ligament/anococcygeal body to supply the skin over the coccyx and between coccyx and anus.
ClinicalCoccydynia (coccygeal pain after trauma/childbirth); contributes to pelvic floor function.

los.text: Identify the obturator nerve and explain that its course is from the medial margin of psoas muscle to the obturator foramen.
los.html:
Obturator nerveFrom the lumbar plexus (anterior divisions of L2, L3, L4) within psoas major.
Course
  • Emerges from the medial border of psoas at the pelvic brim
  • → runs behind the common iliac vessels and lateral to the internal iliac vessels and ureter
  • → along the lateral wall of the pelvis (on obturator internus) with obturator vessels (below it)
  • → passes through the obturator canal (upper part of the obturator foramen, gap in obturator membrane)
  • → divides into anterior and posterior divisions around adductor brevis in the medial thigh.
Supplies
  • Adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, pectineus (sometimes), adductor magnus (adductor part), obturator externus
  • Skin of the medial thigh
  • Hip and knee joints (articular branches → hip pain referred to the knee).
Clinical
  • Injury in pelvic surgery (lymph node dissection), pelvic fractures, childbirth/tumours → weak adduction (wide-based gait), medial thigh numbness
  • Obturator hernia (elderly thin women: Howship–Romberg sign: medial thigh/knee pain)
  • Obturator sign in pelvic appendicitis (internal rotation of flexed hip irritates obturator internus).

los.text: Describe the courses of the principal veins of the leg.
los.html:
Superficial veinCourse
Great saphenous
  • Medial end of dorsal arch
  • → in front of medial malleolus
  • → medial leg
  • → behind medial knee
  • → medial thigh
  • → saphenofemoral junction
Small saphenousLateral end of dorsal arch → behind lateral malleolus → midline calf → saphenopopliteal junction
Deep veinCourse / relations
Posterior tibial, fibular, anterior tibialPaired venae comitantes; posterior tibial behind medial malleolus; plantar veins drain in
PoplitealFormed from the leg veins; in popliteal fossa, superficial to the artery
Femoral
  • Through adductor hiatus and canal into the femoral triangle
  • Medial to femoral artery at inguinal ligament
  • Receives profunda femoris and great saphenous veins
Common femoral → external iliacPasses under the inguinal ligament
Calf sinuses (soleal, gastrocnemius)Drain into posterior tibial/fibular and popliteal veins
  • Valves in all (more numerous distally).
  • Clinical: DVT (usually begins in calf sinuses/valve pockets; proximal (popliteal and above) more likely to embolise)
    • "superficial femoral vein" is a deep vein (use "femoral vein" to avoid confusion)
    • femoral vein access for central lines (medial to arterial pulse).

los.text: Explain the function of the connection of the superficial to the deep veins via the perforator veins and link to the development of varicose veins.
los.html:
Perforator veins
  • Pierce the deep fascia connecting superficial → deep veins (thigh: Dodd/Hunter; knee: Boyd; medial calf: Cockett perforators (ankle perforators))
  • Their valves allow flow only from superficial to deep.
Function
  • Drain superficial venous blood into the deep system so that calf muscle pump can propel it towards the heart
  • Protect superficial veins from the high pressures generated in deep veins during muscle contraction.
Varicose veins
  • Valvular incompetence at the saphenofemoral/saphenopopliteal junctions and/or perforators (primary weakness or post-thrombotic damage)
  • → reflux of blood from deep to superficial veins during calf contraction ("blow-out") and on standing
  • → raised superficial venous pressure
  • → dilatation, elongation and tortuosity of superficial veins (varicosities)
  • → further valve failure (vicious cycle)
  • → chronic venous insufficiency, skin changes and ulceration (especially around incompetent ankle perforators in the gaiter area).

los.text: Explain the mechanisms in the lower limb responsible for venous return to the heart (the muscular venous pump).
los.html:
Calf muscle pump ("peripheral heart")
  • Deep veins and venous sinuses within soleus/gastrocnemius are enclosed by tight deep fascia
  • Muscle contraction (walking, plantarflexion) squeezes them → blood driven upwards (proximal valves open) while distal valves and perforator valves close (preventing backflow and reflux into superficial veins)
  • Relaxation → deep vein pressure falls → blood drawn in from superficial veins (via perforators) and distal veins.
Other mechanisms of venous return
  • Venous valves (one-way flow).
  • Foot pump (plantar venous plexus compressed on weight-bearing).
  • Respiratory pump (inspiration ↓ intrathoracic pressure and ↑ abdominal pressure → draws blood into thorax).
  • Vis a tergo (residual arterial pressure from behind) and vis a fronte (suction from right atrial filling).
  • Arterial pulsation of adjacent arteries (venae comitantes).
  • Venous tone (sympathetic venoconstriction) and gravity (elevation).
Failure(immobility, ankle stiffness, paralysis, valve incompetence, obesity)Venous stasis → DVT, oedema, chronic venous insufficiency. Hence early mobilisation, calf exercises, compression and IPC devices for VTE prevention.

los.text: Describe the boundaries of the femoral triangle and the anatomical relationships of the femoral nerve, artery, vein and lymph nodes to each other and the inguinal ligament, with particular regard to arterial blood sampling and catheter placement
los.html:
• Femoral triangle (upper anterior thigh):
    • Boundaries: superior: inguinal ligament; lateral: medial border of sartorius; medial: medial (or lateral) border of adductor longus; floor: iliopsoas (laterally), pectineus and adductor longus (medially); roof: fascia lata (with saphenous opening/cribriform fascia), superficial fascia, skin.
    • Contents, lateral → medial ("NAVEL"): Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (femoral canal), Lymph nodes (deep inguinal).
    • Femoral sheath holds the artery, vein and canal; the nerve lies outside it.
LandmarkLocationWhat's there
Mid-inguinal pointMidway between ASIS and pubic symphysisFemoral artery passes under the inguinal ligament
Midpoint of inguinal ligamentMidway between ASIS and pubic tubercleDeep inguinal ring
  • Clinical:
    • Arterial blood sampling/femoral artery puncture: palpate pulse at mid-inguinal point, below the inguinal ligament (puncture above → retroperitoneal haemorrhage; too low → bifurcation/pseudoaneurysm); femoral vein is medial to the pulse (central line insertion: "venous is medial"), nerve lateral.
    • Cardiac catheterisation/angiography access (though radial preferred), femoral nerve block (lateral to artery), femoral hernia (through femoral canal below and lateral to pubic tubercle), lymphadenopathy, femoral aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm (after puncture).

los.text: Demonstrate the courses of the major arteries that supply the hip, gluteal region, thigh, leg, ankle and foot.
los.html:
Pelvis/hip/glutealInternal iliac artery → superior gluteal (above piriformis: gluteus medius/minimus) and inferior gluteal (below piriformis: gluteus maximus) arteries, obturator artery (medial thigh; artery of ligamentum teres).
Thigh
  • External iliac
  • → (under inguinal ligament) common femoral artery
  • → gives profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery (posterolateral, ~4 cm below ligament; supplies thigh via medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (hip/femoral head) and perforating arteries (posterior compartment))
  • → continues as femoral (superficial femoral) artery through the adductor canal (Hunter's)
  • → adductor hiatus
  • → popliteal artery.
Knee/leg
  • Popliteal artery (genicular branches around knee)
  • → at lower border of popliteus divides into anterior tibial artery (through interosseous membrane into anterior compartment → becomes dorsalis pedis on dorsum of foot) and tibioperoneal trunk
  • → posterior tibial artery (deep posterior compartment → behind medial malleolus → medial and lateral plantar arteries in sole) and fibular (peroneal) artery (lateral compartment muscles via perforators; lateral ankle).
FootDorsalis pedis → arcuate artery, deep plantar artery joining the plantar arch (from lateral plantar artery).
Clinical
  • Sites of atherosclerosis (common femoral, superficial femoral at adductor canal, popliteal, tibial vessels in diabetes)
  • Popliteal aneurysm
  • Compartment syndrome compromising anterior tibial artery.

los.text: Explain the functional significance of anastomoses between branches of the arteries at the hip and knee.
los.html:
• Anastomoses provide collateral circulation if a main vessel is slowly narrowed/occluded (or ligated)
  • Acute occlusions don't allow time for collaterals to enlarge → severe ischaemia.
Hip region: trochanteric and cruciate anastomoses
  • Trochanteric anastomosis (near trochanteric fossa): superior and inferior gluteal arteries + medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries → supplies femoral head (via retinacular vessels).
  • Cruciate anastomosis (at level of lesser trochanter): inferior gluteal + medial and lateral circumflex femoral + first perforating artery → links internal iliac with femoral/profunda systems → bypasses occlusion of external iliac or common femoral artery.
Knee: genicular anastomosis
  • Vessels: medial and lateral superior/inferior genicular arteries (popliteal), descending genicular (femoral), descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral, anterior tibial recurrent, circumflex fibular.
  • Bypasses femoral/popliteal occlusion: e.g. SFA occlusion at the adductor canal may cause only claudication.
Clinical
  • Collaterals explain why chronic PAD often presents with claudication rather than gangrene
  • Femoral neck fractures disrupt retinacular supply (AVN) despite anastomoses
  • Popliteal artery injury (knee dislocation) → poor collaterals → high amputation risk if not repaired quickly.

los.text: Demonstrate the locations at which the femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses may be felt and predict the effects of arterial pathology.
los.html:
PulseLocation
FemoralMid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis), just below inguinal ligament
Popliteal
  • Deep in popliteal fossa: patient supine, knee slightly flexed (~30°, relaxed), fingertips of both hands pressing anteriorly against the posterior tibia/femur
  • Hard to feel (easily felt = popliteal aneurysm)
Dorsalis pedisDorsum of foot, lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon, over navicular/intermediate cuneiform; absent in ~5–10% of normal people
Posterior tibialPosterior and inferior to medial malleolus (halfway between medial malleolus and heel/Achilles)
  • Predicting effects of arterial pathology:
    • Aorto-iliac disease: ↓/absent femoral pulses and all distal pulses; buttock/thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction (Leriche).
    • Femoropopliteal (superficial femoral) disease: femoral present, popliteal and foot pulses absent → calf claudication.
    • Tibial/infrapopliteal disease (diabetes): femoral and popliteal present, foot pulses absent → foot ischaemia, ulcers.
    • Acute embolism: sudden loss of pulses distal to embolus lodgement (often at bifurcations: common femoral, popliteal trifurcation), normal pulses on contralateral side.
    • Aneurysm: expansile pulses (AAA, popliteal: can thrombose/embolise → acute ischaemia).

los.text: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the lower limb and its relationship to tumour spread.
los.html:
• Superficial lymphatics of the lower limb follow superficial veins: medial group along great saphenous vein → superficial inguinal nodes (vertical group along terminal GSV; horizontal group below inguinal ligament)
    • lateral/posterior heel and lateral foot lymphatics follow small saphenous vein → popliteal nodes.
  • Deep lymphatics follow deep vessels
    • → popliteal nodes
    • → deep inguinal nodes (medial to femoral vein; uppermost = Cloquet's node in femoral canal)
    • → external iliac nodes
    • → common iliac
    • → para-aortic
    • → cisterna chyli/thoracic duct.
  • Superficial inguinal nodes also drain: skin of lower abdominal wall below umbilicus
    • buttock
    • perineum
    • external genitalia (scrotal skin, vulva, lower vagina)
    • anal canal below pectinate line
    • superolateral uterus (via round ligament, minor).
    • Not the testes (→ para-aortic).
  • Tumour spread: melanoma or SCC of foot/leg → popliteal/inguinal nodes
    • anal SCC, vulval/penile cancer → inguinal nodes
    • inguinal lymphadenopathy prompts examination of the whole lower limb, perineum, genitals and anus
    • sentinel lymph node biopsy (melanoma, vulval cancer)
    • inguinal node dissection → lymphoedema of leg
    • infection (cellulitis, STIs: LGV, syphilis) → reactive inguinal nodes.

los.text: Interpret standard diagnostic images of the lower limb and be able to recognise common abnormalities.
los.html:
Standard images
  • X-rays of hip/pelvis (AP pelvis + lateral hip), femur, knee (AP, lateral, skyline), tibia/fibula, ankle (AP/mortise, lateral), foot (AP, oblique, lateral)
  • CT (complex fractures), MRI (occult fractures, soft tissue, AVN), USS (DVT, effusions, Baker's cyst), duplex/CTA (arteries).
Common abnormalities
  • Hip: femoral neck fracture (Shenton's line disruption), intertrochanteric fracture, OA (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts), AVN (crescent sign, collapse), SUFE (children: Klein's line), Perthes, DDH, dislocation, Paget's, metastases.
  • Knee: OA (medial compartment narrowing), tibial plateau fracture (lipohaemarthrosis), patellar fracture vs bipartite patella, effusion, chondrocalcinosis (CPPD), Segond fracture (ACL tear association), osteochondritis dissecans, tumours (osteosarcoma: metaphysis, sunburst periosteal reaction, Codman's triangle).
  • Ankle/foot: Weber fractures, talar shift, 5th metatarsal base avulsion vs Jones fracture, Lisfranc injury (widening between 1st/2nd metatarsal bases), calcaneal fracture (Böhler's angle ↓), stress fractures, gout erosions (1st MTP), Charcot foot, osteomyelitis (diabetic foot).
  • Long bones: fractures, periosteal reaction, lytic/sclerotic lesions (metastases, myeloma), osteomyelitis, Paget's (thickened cortex, bowing).
ApproachSystematic (as LO 48), compare sides, correlate with clinical findings.
